abstract: This study systematically examines how well AI agent benchmarks reflect real-world human work by analyzing 43 benchmarks and 72,342 tasks across 1,016 U.S. occupations. The authors find substantial mismatches between agent development efforts, which tend to be programming-centric, and the actual distribution of human labor and economic value. They characterize agent utility by autonomy levels and propose three principles—coverage, realism, and granular evaluation—for designing benchmarks that better capture socially important and technically challenging forms of work.
keyFindings: Analysis of 43 benchmarks containing 72,342 tasks reveals substantial mismatches between agent development focus and real-world labor market distribution across 1,016 U.S. occupations.
Agent development efforts are disproportionately programming-centric compared to where human labor and economic value are actually concentrated.
Current agent benchmarks show limited alignment with human employment and capital allocation patterns in the broader labor market.
Agent autonomy levels vary significantly across different work scenarios, requiring different interaction strategies.
Three measurable principles—coverage, realism, and granular evaluation—are proposed for designing benchmarks that better reflect socially important and technically challenging work.
methodology: Systematic analysis of 43 AI agent benchmarks containing 72,342 tasks mapped to work domains and skills. Comparison of benchmark task distribution against 1,016 real-world U.S. occupations using employment and capital allocation data. Assessment of agent autonomy levels across targeted work areas.
